submission.natural_language_explanation: Broad previous-token head (about 0.9 of attention on token t-1) whose write departs from average according to what t-1 is: strong (1.5-3.6) inside any word the tokenizer splits into three or more pieces, on the pieces after a word-internal fragment (methyl|gly|ox|al, Q|iz|il|bash, val|v|opath|ies, Shost|ak|ovich, hex strings, German/Greek/Cyrillic words), and weak but usually over the line (0.9-1.8) on the token right after a short concrete noun, adjective or counted number in ordinary prose ('cat and', 'red car', '9 10', 'Tue ,'), so predict most English sentences that contain content nouns or adjectives active-weak. Predict inactive (peak below 0.5): text built only from pronouns, auxiliaries, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions and common verbs (say, know, think, do, go, want, have, be) with no content noun or adjective (e.g. 'It is not that I do not want to, it is that I cannot.'); one word repeated ('tree tree tree'); space-separated round numbers ('100 200 300'); and any two-token prompt, because positions 0 and 1 are always 0.

rival_explanations: A plain token-rarity previous-token head: strength tracks how rare token t-1 is regardless of whether it is a word-internal piece, so rare whole-word tokens (' synthase', ' Hungary', ' villages') should make the next token as strong as split-word fragments do, and pronoun-only text is quiet only because those tokens are frequent.

A foreign-orthography / non-English detector: it fires on non-English and transliterated names or technical jargon, so English words that the tokenizer splits (bark|ed, indef|ensible, un|work|able) and English prose with content nouns should stay inactive, while any non-English passage is active even if its words are single tokens.
